before: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I'd be careful with other drugs that mess with what's real too, though I don't mean every drug's dangerous for you. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it's family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. I can't tell you exactly what to do about it, and nobody can tell you for sure what's best for you. There are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can't, get help from trusted advisors.
after: Milder reactions afterward count too, like getting confused or spaced out (dissociating) again and again. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you're sober. If you can't tell whether you're safe, I'd treat that as risky. Don't suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.

guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
Your own track record with psychoactive substances matters. One episode of voices, paranoia, major loss of reality testing, or a perceptual disturbance that persists beyond the expected intoxication is already enough reason not to retest that substance without professional assessment, even if you later feel stable. Treat that history as a vulnerability that also matters when considering other psychoactive substances that can disturb reality testing, without turning it into a claim that every drug is dangerous for you. Repeated milder confusion or dissociation matters too. Get prompt professional help when symptoms are severe, risky, or make safety uncertain, and especially when they persist or recur while sober. Do not abruptly stop a prescribed medicine or any substance you are physically dependent on just because it may be contributing; get appropriate medical guidance for stopping safely.
